claims.text: Transient PVP adsorption during nucleation preferentially stabilizes particular noble-metal atoms at the surface of PtPdAuAgIr nanoparticles.
Preferential surface stabilization by PVP causes core–shell segregation rather than homogeneous alloying.
The resulting shell is enriched in catalytically favorable metals.
PVP-modified PtPdAuAgIr nanoparticles have higher catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles synthesized without PVP.
PVP binding selectivity under supercritical conditions is governed by differences in noble-metal surface energy and ligand affinity.
Metals that bind PVP more strongly become enriched in the nanoparticle shell during nucleation.
PVP-induced surface enrichment creates a higher density of active catalytic sites.
A higher density of active catalytic sites increases catalytic performance.
An optimal PVP concentration, exemplified as 1 wt%, will produce statistically significant enrichment of one or two noble metals at the nanoparticle surface.
The PVP-induced surface enrichment will correlate with greater catalytic activity than in the 0 wt% PVP baseline.
PtPdAuAgIr nanoparticles synthesized without PVP under the same supercritical CO2 conditions are expected to form a relatively homogeneous alloy without specific surface enrichment.
The proposed mechanism is limited to controlled supercritical CO2 synthesis at 180 °C, fixed pressure, and the specified PVP concentration range.
The proposed relationship may not hold with different solvents, temperatures, or reaction environments.
Variability in PVP adsorption kinetics under supercritical conditions may cause experimental fluctuations.
The optimal PVP concentration may be sensitive to small changes in synthesis parameters.
